title: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget.
ballot_label: Caption: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city’s annual discretionary budget. Question: Should Portland create participatory budgeting program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2% of city’s discretionary budget?
summary: A citizen-initiated Portland charter amendment requiring the City Council to allocate an amount equal to at least 2% of the city's adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses to a participatory budgeting program. Residents could propose citywide or district projects; city staff and budget delegates would refine proposals, and residents would make binding selections. An oversight committee of residents would help develop the program, which would start July 2027.
yes_means: A yes vote amends the Portland City Charter to create a participatory budgeting program in which residents make binding decisions on spending an amount equal to at least 2% of the city's discretionary budget.
no_means: A no vote leaves the current budget process unchanged, in which the Mayor proposes and the Council amends and adopts the budget.
fiscal_impact: Under a recent forecast, the ballot summary gives a preliminary estimate of $16.4 million in FY 2027-28 and $17.0 million in FY 2028-29 to be allocated to the program; Council may identify funding from the entire city budget to meet the obligation.

arguments.author: Devin Ruiz, deputy director, NextUp Action Fund
arguments.statement: Devin Ruiz of NextUp Action Fund, which helped fund the measure's committee, says the measure gives Portlanders a direct way to push back on cuts and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.
arguments.excerpt: Your 2 Cents gives Portlanders a direct way to push back and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.

source.publisher: Willamette Week

arguments.author: Jim Labbe, chief petitioner; executive director, Participatory Budgeting Oregon
arguments.statement: Chief petitioner Jim Labbe says Portland has a public trust crisis about how it spends money and that participatory budgeting is a demonstrated bottom-up mechanism to address it.
arguments.excerpt: It's got to be from the bottom up, and participatory budgeting is really a demonstrated mechanism to do that.

source.publisher: Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB)

arguments.author: Jim Labbe, chief petitioner; executive director, Participatory Budgeting Oregon
arguments.statement: Labbe says a recurring process in which residents register priorities and create data to inform the budget is the missing piece.
arguments.excerpt: "Having a recurring process in which residents can register their priorities and create data to inform the budget," Labbe said. "That's the missing piece."

source.publisher: Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB)

arguments.author: Mayor Keith Wilson
arguments.statement: Mayor Keith Wilson says the measure would write a permanent budget set-aside into the charter that no future mayor or council could adjust.
arguments.excerpt: No future mayor or council could adjust it.

source.publisher: Willamette Week

arguments.author: Mayor Keith Wilson
arguments.statement: Wilson says the measure would take at least $16 million a year from the fund that pays for shelter beds, park maintenance and investigators, and that Portland cannot afford it.
arguments.excerpt: Wilson said in a statement the measure would pull “at least $16 million a year from the fund that pays for shelter beds, park maintenance, and investigators, and [hand] it to a process the measure doesn’t even define,” something “Portland can’t afford,” he wrote.

source.publisher: Willamette Week

arguments.author: Laurie Wimmer, executive secretary-treasurer, Northwest Oregon Labor Council; chair, Protect Our City Services PAC
arguments.statement: Laurie Wimmer, who chairs the opposing committee Protect Our City Services, says the measure would take millions from parks, community centers, Portland Street Response, firefighting and other services.
arguments.excerpt: take millions away from parks, community centers, Portland Street Response, firefighting, and other essential services

source.publisher: Willamette Week

arguments.author: Max Steele
arguments.statement: Max Steele's argument in favor urges a yes vote, saying the measure would likely create one of the largest participatory budgets in the country.
arguments.excerpt: You should vote yes on what is likely to be one of the largest participatory budgets in the country.

source.publisher: Multnomah County Elections (Nov 3, 2026 Voters' Pamphlet, p. M-79)

arguments.author: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX
arguments.statement: The Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX argument says the measure does not raise taxes and lets Portlanders help choose what their neighborhoods need most.
arguments.excerpt: This measure does not raise taxes. A Yes vote for Measure 26-267 lets Portlanders help choose what our neighborhoods need most.

source.publisher: Multnomah County Elections (Nov 3, 2026 Voters' Pamphlet, p. M-79)

arguments.author: Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX
arguments.statement: The Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX frequently-asked-questions argument says the measure does not raise taxes and gives Portlanders a greater say in how existing city funds are spent.
arguments.excerpt: Measure 26-267 does not raise taxes. It simply gives Portlanders a greater say in how existing city funds are spent.

source.publisher: Multnomah County Elections (Nov 3, 2026 Voters' Pamphlet, p. M-80)

arguments.author: Tony Morse, Protect Our City Services
arguments.statement: Protect Our City Services cites a City Club of Portland report that described charter-mandated participatory budgeting as nearly unprecedented and difficult to justify from the available evidence.
arguments.excerpt: Proposals to adopt and institutionalize PB as a city-wide program funded through a charter change or citizen initiative appear to be nearly unprecedented in the U.S. and difficult to justify from the available evidence about PB’s benefits.

source.publisher: Multnomah County Elections (Nov 3, 2026 Voters' Pamphlet, p. M-85)

arguments.author: Bob Weinstein (with Mike Lindberg and Vadim Mozyrsky)
arguments.statement: Bob Weinstein, with Mike Lindberg and Vadim Mozyrsky, argues the charter amendment would require the city to direct at least 2% of discretionary spending, initially $16 million, to participatory budgeting.
arguments.excerpt: The proposal would amend Portland’s Charter to require the city to forever hand over at least 2% of discretionary spending — initially $16 million— to a participatory budgeting process, no matter what else the city needs.

source.publisher: Multnomah County Elections (Nov 3, 2026 Voters' Pamphlet, p. M-86)

arguments.author: Jason Williams, Taxpayers Association of Oregon
arguments.statement: The Taxpayers Association of Oregon argues the program would spend $16 to $17 million a year through a process separate from the Council's normal budget hearings.
arguments.excerpt: The City’s own estimate puts this program at $16.4 million in FY 2027-28 and $17.0 million the year after — spent through a process separate from the Council’s normal budget hearings.

source.publisher: Multnomah County Elections (Nov 3, 2026 Voters' Pamphlet, p. M-86)

gaps: Arguments printed in the county voters' pamphlet (Multnomah, M-79 to M-91): 15 in favor and 15 in opposition. The 6-per-side cap is filled by the 3 existing news-sourced arguments plus the first 3 pamphlet arguments per side in pamphlet order; the other 12 in favor and 12 in opposition are not itemized.

Omitted in favor (pamphlet order): Healthy Democracy; Portland Small Businesses; East Portland Residents; Black-led Organizations & Black Leaders; Portland Democratic Socialists of America; three political-science professors; and six others, all but one furnished by Edward Kurtz, Yes on Your 2 Cents PDX (M-79 to M-85).

Omitted in opposition (pamphlet order): Portland Firefighters' Association (M-87); NW Oregon Labor Council (M-87); Portland Police Association (M-88); Mayor Keith Wilson (M-88); City Councilors (M-88); Future Portland Action Fund (M-91); and six others furnished by Protect Our City Services, Taxpayers Association of Oregon and others (M-86 to M-91).
No explanatory statement was filed for this measure (county pamphlet M-78).
collection_notes: Updated 2026-10-16 from the Multnomah County voters' pamphlet extract (pages M-78 to M-91; cited by source_url and printed page). Ballot title text matches the existing ballot_label. The Washington County pamphlet edition (WC-51 to WC-54) also prints this measure, with fewer arguments; consulted, not cited. Max Steele's argument is filed 'in favor' but is written in a sarcastic tone that reads as opposition; it is included because it is the first filed argument in favor, attributed only to its literal vote-yes statement. Existing news-sourced arguments (y1-y3, n1-n3) are kept; the validator caps arguments at 6 per side so only 3 pamphlet arguments per side are itemized. The Sept 8, 2026 argument deadline has passed per the county filings page. Measure document PDFs on multco.us (measure_26-26x/download, referral documents) have no machine-readable text (scanned). WebFetch limits quotes to 125 characters, so several excerpts are sentence segments. yes_means/no_means are not official text: Oregon local ballot titles have no official result-of-vote statement, so they are neutral one-sentence descriptions written strictly from the official ballot question. Inventory title, number (26-267) and jurisdiction (City of Portland) match the multco.us page and filings list (filed 8/28/2026; ballot title submitted by Louise Hansen, City Elections Officer). Per inventory, the measure also appears in Washington and Clackamas county lists. Willamette Week pages did not display a publication date; published_at is taken from the URL path. The Oct 7, 2026 WW article returned a server error on three attempts. The yes committee is reported as Your 2 Cents PDX; no committee website was linked from a T1/T3 page, so none is cited.
